title: Iris and Comet's River Rescue
markdown:
The sun burst over the peaks. Birdsong erupted. Iris bounced up, energy zinging. Today felt special. Her dog, Comet, tail a frantic whip, nudged her hand, amber eyes bright.

“Ready for anything, Comet?” Iris grinned, grabbing her vest. The air was crisp, smelling of mint and damp earth. Dew flashed on the grass like someone had scattered beads and forgotten them.

Ranger Elowen’s comm crackled. “Iris! Comet! Urgent retrieval! The weather drone is down near the old willow! The current’s fierce. We need it now!”

In a flash they sprinted. The river churned brown, a relentless rush. There, tangled mid-stream, bobbed Nimbus 7, precarious as a thought you might lose.

“Oh no!” Iris cried. Comet whined. The drone was heavy, waterlogged. Pulling it straight risked losing it to the pull.

Iris scanned the bank. A twig floated. A stone sank, quick and unapologetic. The drone? Almost sinking. What made the difference? She watched the twig bob, cheerful as a small boat. Then the stone plunged.

An idea sparked. “Comet, fetch that sturdy branch!”

While Comet bounded off, all legs and good intentions, Iris tied rope to the drone. She secured the other end to a hollow testing tube and dropped it in. The tube bobbed, pulling gently, a polite insistence. Next she filled a metal canteen halfway and tied it to the rope, past the tube.

“The tube keeps the drone from sinking too deep,” she told Comet, who was already supervising with his whole face. “The canteen acts as a counterweight. Buoyancy and displacement. The tube pushes water aside and floats because it’s less dense. The canteen helps us control the pull.”

With Comet nudging her, Iris lowered the canteen and let the rope slide. The testing tube danced, drawing Nimbus 7 slowly toward the bank. Churning water slapped. The rope felt slick. Damp earth rose in the air. Inch by careful inch they guided their cargo, not yanking, not panicking, just persuading.

They reached shallow water. The drone was safe, dripping and undignified, which was still better than gone.

Ranger Elowen appeared, boots wet to the lace. “Iris! How?”

Iris beamed, then the brightness softened. The river kept going, brown and busy, as if it had never nearly stolen anything. “Buoyancy, Ranger. The tube displaced water and floated. Things float if they’re less dense than the water they push aside. Density and displacement.”

“Amazing,” Elowen said, already kneeling to check Nimbus 7’s battered fins. “Vital knowledge.”

Iris patted Comet. His fur was river-cold. The morning was still young, and the drone would fly again, and something in her chest held both the triumph and the near-miss at once.

“There’s so much to discover,” she said. “I wonder what else the world can teach us.”
characters: Iris (an environmental scout), Comet (an amber-eyed lurcher), Ranger Elowen (a river-rescue ranger)
author: StoryGen Community
